slides.text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are an important part of the deep learning revolution.
The design of CNNs is partly motivated by the visual cortex.
Hubel and Wiesel's studies showed that first-level neurons in the visual cortex activate for simple shapes.
Hubel and Wiesel's studies showed that second-level neurons in the visual cortex activate for combinations of simple shapes.
Hubel and Wiesel did not study third-level neurons.
Information from the retina goes to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), then to the visual cortex.
The visual cortex is neatly organised into layers, from V1 to V4 and then either to V5 or to V6.
V1 processes local features.
V2 processes more local features and binocular vision.
V3 processes colour, texture, and first results of segmentation.
V4 processes geometric shapes and silhouettes.
V4 is the most important layer for attention.
V5 recognises motion of objects segmented in V4.
V6 generalises data from the whole image.
V6 is involved in wide-field stimulation.
V6 processes changes due to our own movement.
V7 (controversial) is involved in recognition of complex objects, e.g., human faces.
The 'what' pathway goes from V2 to V4 and is for recognition of shapes and objects.
The 'where' pathway goes from V2 to V5 and V6 and is for motion recognition and control over eyes and hands.
Biological ideas about layered visual processing are reflected in artificial neural networks as convolutional networks.
Convolutions first appeared in the Neocognitron by Fukushima in 1979 and 1980.
The modern form of convolutions appeared in LeCun's group in the late 1980s.
The main idea of CNNs is to apply the same operation to every part of the image.
In CNNs, the picture is broken into windows.
In CNNs, a small neural network is applied to every window.
In CNNs, the image is compressed by max-pooling over small windows.
In CNNs, prediction is done with a fully connected network.
Adding new layers to a CNN improves generalisation.
In CNNs, we can see where exactly in the picture individual neurons activate.
In CNNs, formally, we have a single small matrix (weight kernel) that is applied to every window.
A two-dimensional convolution with a kernel of size (2d+1)×(2d+1) and weight matrix W is defined as y^{(l)}_{i,j} = sum_{-d ≤ a,b ≤ d} W_{a,b} x^{(l)}_{i+a, j+b}.
The convolution output is usually followed by a nonlinearity h: z^{(l)}_{i,j} = h(y^{(l)}_{i,j}).
In modern networks, the nonlinearity is almost always ReLU, defined as z^{(l)}_{i,j} = max(0, y^{(l)}_{i,j}).
After the nonlinearity, max-pooling is applied, defined as x^{(l+1)}_{i,j} = max_{-d ≤ a,b ≤ d} z^{(l)}_{i+a, j+b}.
Sometimes average-pooling is used instead of max-pooling, but max-pooling is usual.
The sequence of convolution, nonlinearity, and pooling constitutes one convolutional layer.
LeNet is a classical early example of a CNN architecture.
Modern CNNs can become very deep thanks to a number of architectural tricks and advances.

transcript.text: A neural network is a large computational graph built from elementary operations.
A neural network receives two kinds of inputs: the actual input (e.g., an image) and the weights.
The graph's output is a loss function $L(x, y, w)$, with the correct answer $y$ provided at the end.
The overall loss $L(w)$ is the average of per-example losses over a mini-batch.
Weights are updated by gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla_w L$.
In practice, more sophisticated optimizers such as Adam are used instead of vanilla gradient descent.
An architecture is the structure of the computational graph of a neural network.
The computational graph must be a directed acyclic graph (no cycles) so that it can be traversed topologically forward and backward.
Each node in the graph must implement forward and backward propagation computations.
A common organization of neural networks is a layered architecture.
A layer is a set of neurons (perceptrons) that mostly connect to neurons of the next layer.
The concept of a layer is informal and admits skip connections that bypass layers, such as residual connections.
The simplest class of neural networks is feed-forward fully connected networks.
In a fully connected layer, neurons do not connect to each other inside the layer; they receive inputs from all neurons of the previous layer and send outputs to all neurons of the next layer.
Fully connected layers form a complete bipartite graph between successive layers.
The final layers of a network typically reduce to a smaller set of neurons to produce the output.
Fully connected layers remain important and appear in transformers and other architectures.
Artificial neural networks were inspired by the brain and connectionism.
The human brain cannot perform gradient descent.
A biological neuron has many dendrites and a single axon, and can compute only one function (the forward pass).
Gradient descent requires each node to compute at least two functions: forward propagation and backward propagation to compute gradients.
Since biological neurons cannot run a backward pass, the brain must use a different learning mechanism.
That learning mechanism must somehow send a signal back from the ultimate goal (the loss) to every neuron, implying that the brain must have loops to propagate error signals.
The biological brain requires extensive feedback connections for training.
The brain does have feedback connections.
The analogy between biological neurons and artificial neural networks ends at the point of feedback connections.
A single neuron or perceptron is a good model of a biological neuron, especially with ReLU activations.
The brain uses connectionism—composing many simple functions to produce complex behavior.
The brain definitely does not use gradient descent.
The brain's architecture is fundamentally different from that of artificial neural networks.
The brain has layers, but between every two layers there are feedback connections that go back, and from later layers there are connections that go all the way back.
We do not understand the brain's fine architecture in detail.
We know general regions like the visual cortex and its gross layers.
The fine structure of the brain is extremely difficult to ascertain.
Hubel and Wiesel won the Nobel Prize for their studies of the visual cortex.
Convolutional networks are partly motivated by the visual cortex, but the analogy eventually ends.
In the 1960s and 1970s, Hubel and Wiesel made famous studies of the visual cortex.
Their key advantage was a device of tiny electrodes that could be attached to a single neuron in a live brain to read its activation.
Before that, researchers could only infer brain function from stroke patients' deficits.
Hubel and Wiesel attached electrodes to individual neurons in a cat's brain to see what each neuron responds to.
The visual cortex receives visual input via the optic nerve from the eyes.
The first layer of neurons in the visual cortex takes immediate input from the eyes.
These first-layer neurons have small receptive fields, each looking at a small part of the entire picture.

These neurons recognize very simple shapes, and their response is orientation-selective; for example, a neuron might fire strongly for a bright vertical line, and its activation drops to near zero if the line is rotated.
A second layer of neurons combines simple shapes into more complex ones.
A neuron detecting vertical lines and another detecting horizontal lines could feed into a neuron that detects a corner.
Hubel and Wiesel found such combination-detecting neurons in the second layer.
The brain's structure becomes extremely messy beyond the second layer, so they did not go further.
The visual cortex layers (V1, V2, V4, V5, etc.) are not a clean feedforward network; they have extensive feedback and interconnections.
A diagram of the most important neural pathways in early visual cortex shows a clear first and second layer, but beyond that a tangled mess.
The observation that simple geometric shapes combine hierarchically inspired attempts to imitate this in computers.
Convolutional networks are an old idea, dating back at least to the neocognitron by Kunihiko Fukushima in the late 1970s.
The neocognitron used several layers and convolution operations.
The neocognitron used ReLU-like hinge activations.
The neocognitron's filters were hand-crafted and not trainable; it lacked a learning algorithm.
Yann LeCun's group developed the modern trainable convolutional network starting in the late 1980s.
Convolutional networks are an example of structural regularization.
The main assumption behind CNNs is that the same feature-detecting function is applied everywhere in the image.
Because the local inputs differ, the function's output varies across locations.
In CNNs, the input image is broken into small, typically overlapping windows (tiles).
For every tile, a small neural network is applied.
The small network is trained via gradient descent and has weights.
The small network is applied only to the little tile of a few pixels.
The exact same small network is applied to every tile (weight sharing).
Each tile yields an output vector of several features.
The output vectors inherit the geometric ordering of the input windows, retaining width and height, and forming a 3D tensor with depth (features).
Inputs to a convolutional layer also have depth; for example, a color image has depth 3.
A convolutional layer maps one 3D tensor to another.

Multiple convolutional layers can be stacked by applying the same operation to the output tensor: tiling spatial dimensions, applying a small network to each tile, and producing another feature tensor.
In deep learning, these multi-dimensional arrays are called tensors.
Classical CNNs and many modern architectures use pooling layers in addition to convolutional layers.
A feature in a convolutional layer has a receptive field, which is the region of the original input that influences it.
With 3×3 convolutional tiles, a feature's receptive field is initially 3×3.
Each additional 3×3 convolutional layer adds 2 to the height and width of the receptive field (e.g., from 3×3 to 5×5).
To achieve a receptive field covering a 256×256 image with only 3×3 convolutions, you would need around 130 layers.
Using only convolutional layers to cover large images is impractical because it would require excessively deep networks.
Pooling layers are used to reduce spatial dimensions faster than stacking convolutions alone.
A pooling layer takes a feature map, slices it into non-overlapping windows (typically 2×2), and replaces the values in each window with a single value according to a rule.
The two common pooling rules are max pooling (taking the maximum) and average pooling (taking the average).
Max pooling is far more common in practice than average pooling.
Max pooling encourages convolutional layers to extract more meaningful features.
For a feature detector that outputs 1 where a target is present and 0 elsewhere, max pooling over a region yields 1 if the target appears anywhere, while average pooling would be diluted by zeros.
Features detecting object presence suit max pooling, while average features like color suit averaging.
Because CNNs focus on detecting shapes and objects, max pooling is typical.
Alternating convolution and pooling layers rapidly reduces spatial geometry.
With 2×2 pooling, each pooling layer halves the width and height, reducing the total number of values by a factor of 4.
After pooling, another convolutional layer can be applied.
The term 'convolution' in CNNs means tiling the input with small windows and independently applying the same transformation to each window.
In practice, a 'convolutional layer' typically uses the simplest transformation: a single fully connected layer applied to each tile.
For a 3D input of size W×H×D, a tile of size w×h×D is cut, always taking all D feature channels.
The tile is flattened to a vector of length D·w·h.
This vector is multiplied by a weight matrix W of shape (D w h)×d' to produce an output vector of dimension d'.
Weight sharing means the same weight matrix W is used for every tile.
The number of parameters in a convolutional layer is D w h d', which depends only on tile size, not on input width or height.
If the input image size is doubled, the same weights are used, and the convolution is simply applied across the larger image.
In practice, the weight matrix of a convolutional layer is stored as a four-dimensional tensor of shape $D \times w \times h \times d'$ rather than as a huge 2D matrix.
In PyTorch, the convolutional layer's weight tensor has dimensions $D \times w \times h \times d'$.
The input to a convolutional layer is a 3D tensor of shape $D \times w \times h$, matching the first three dimensions of the weight tensor.
The output of a convolutional layer is a feature map with depth $d'$.
Convolutional layers are not limited to 2D images.
Convolutional layers can be defined for any kind of input.
Text can be represented as a 2D input of shape $L \times D$, where $L$ is the sequence length and $D$ is the token vector dimension.
A 1D convolution over text slides a window of length $l$ over the sequence to extract a tile of size $l \times D$, flattens the tile, and multiplies it by a shared weight matrix.
For a sequence input, the convolutional weight tensor has shape $D \times l \times d'$, and the output per window is a vector of size $d'$.

For video input, which is a sequence of images, the input tensor has shape $d \times w \times h \times t$, and the convolutional weight tensor is five-dimensional of shape $t \times w \times h \times d \times d'$.
The core idea of convolutional layers—tiling the input and processing each tile with shared weights—applies to inputs of any dimension.
Convolutions were especially productive for images.
All examples in this class will use images.
In convolutional layers, the terms feature maps, channels, and depth all refer to the same thing.
In the LeNet example, the input is a $32 \times 32$ grayscale image with depth 1.
In the LeNet example, the input tensor has shape $1 \times 32 \times 32$.
Without padding, when you cover the input by overlapping tiles, the border pixels cannot be the center of a full tile.
With a $3 \times 3$ filter and no padding, a $32 \times 32$ input would yield a $30 \times 30$ output.
In the LeNet example, the reduction from $32 \times 32$ to $28 \times 28$ indicates a $5 \times 5$ filter.
In the first convolutional layer of LeNet, the weight tensor has shape $1 \times 5 \times 5 \times 6$, giving $5 \times 5 \times 6 = 150$ trainable weights (ignoring biases).
If the same transformation were done with a fully connected layer, the weight matrix would have size $1024 \times 4704$, i.e., about 4.8 million weights.
The convolutional layer reduces the number of weights from about 4.8 million to 150, a huge saving.
Convolutional layers act as a structural regularizer by applying the same weights to every input window, which heavily compresses the hypothesis space.
In LeNet, after the first convolutional layer, a pooling layer with $2 \times 2$ windows reduces the tensor from $6 \times 28 \times 28$ to $6 \times 14 \times 14$.
Max pooling selects the maximum value from each $2 \times 2$ window.
Max pooling has no trainable weights.
In LeNet, the second pooling layer outputs a $6 \times 14 \times 14$ tensor, which is passed to another convolutional layer that outputs a $16 \times 10 \times 10$ tensor.
The second convolutional layer in LeNet has a weight tensor of shape $6 \times 5 \times 5 \times 16$, resulting in $6 \times 5 \times 5 \times 16 = 2400$ trainable weights.

After another pooling layer in LeNet, the tensor has shape $16 \times 5 \times 5$, and since the spatial dimensions are exactly $5 \times 5$, the subsequent layer can be viewed as either convolutional or fully connected.
The classification head of LeNet consists of layers producing 120 features, then 84 features, and finally a 10-class output.
The first fully connected layer in the LeNet head has $16 \times 5 \times 5 \times 120 = 48,000$ weights.
The next fully connected layer has approximately $120 \times 84 = 10,080$ weights.
In classical convolutional networks, after downsampling, the network ends with a few fully connected layers, collectively called the classification head.
In classical convolutional networks, the classification head (the final fully connected layers) holds the vast majority of the total weights.
For example, in LeNet, about 57,000–58,000 of the 60,000 weights are in the head.
In a convolutional network, the convolutional layers perform feature extraction.
During backpropagation, a shared weight in a convolutional layer appears multiple times in the computational graph, and its gradient is the sum of the per-occurrence gradients.
The redundancy of weight sharing makes ReLU activations suitable because sparsity from zeroing some activations does not harm training, as the weight still gets updates from other tiles.
Without padding, a $K \times K$ convolution reduces the spatial dimensions from $W \times H$ to $W-K \times H-K$.
Padding the input with zeros preserves the spatial dimensions after convolution, allowing stacked layers without size reduction.
With zero padding, border pixels can be the center of a convolution window because zeros are imagined outside the image.
Two common padding methods are zero padding and mirror padding.
Zero padding can create implausible features at the border because the convolution window includes many zeros.
Mirror padding copies edge pixels outward as a mirror to avoid the artifact of implausible border features.
The purpose of padding is to allow any input pixel to be the center of a convolution tile.
Using a stride greater than 1 reduces the number of tiles: e.g., stride 2 reduces the number of tiles by a factor of 4, yielding an output size of roughly $W/2 \times H/2$.
With stride 2, every pixel is still included in at least one tile, so no information is lost.
Skipping pixels is called using a stride; stride 1 tiles every pixel, stride 2 skips every other pixel.
A convolutional layer is defined by its weight tensor shape $d \times w \times h \times d'$ (input depth $d$, output depth $d'$), padding, and stride.
The stride can be two-dimensional (e.g., 2 along x and 3 along y), but usually the same stride is used in both dimensions.
The stride controls the tiling pattern, and the weight tensor's output depth $d'$ determines the number of output feature maps.
Using a stride greater than 1 reduces the number of processing steps each pixel participates in, which may be undesirable.
The trend in convolutional networks has been to use pooling less often because it can disrupt computational paths and distort gradients.
Modern architectures like Inception and ResNet often reduce spatial dimensions using strided convolutions within a subnetwork instead of simple pooling.

summary.text: A neural network is a large computational graph composed of elementary operations.
It receives two kinds of inputs: the actual data and the trainable weights.
The graph's final output is a scalar loss L(x, y, w), evaluated by comparing the prediction with the correct answer y.
The total loss over a mini-batch L(w) is the average of the per-example losses.
The weights are updated by gradient descent.
In practice, the weights are updated by more sophisticated optimizers such as Adam.
The weight update formula is w ← w - η ∇_w L.
The deep learning loop consists of forward pass, loss computation, backward pass, and weight update.
When designing a network, we choose its architecture.
The architecture is the structure of the computational graph.
The computational graph must be a directed acyclic graph.
The requirement for a directed acyclic graph is so that it can be traversed topologically forward and backward.
Every node in the computational graph must provide a forward propagation computation.
Every node in the computational graph must provide a backward propagation computation.
A common organization of neural networks is the layered architecture.
A layer is an informal set of neurons that mostly connect to neurons of adjacent layers.
Layers may be skipped by skip (residual) connections.
The simplest class of layered architecture is the feed-forward fully connected network.
In a feed-forward fully connected network, inside a layer, neurons do not connect to each other.
In a feed-forward fully connected network, each neuron receives inputs from all neurons of the previous layer.
In a feed-forward fully connected network, each neuron sends outputs to all neurons of the next layer.
A feed-forward fully connected network forms a complete bipartite graph between successive layers.
Fully connected layers remain important and appear in modern architectures such as transformers.
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are one of the most influential architecture families.
The origin of CNNs is partly biological.
The biological analogy for CNNs eventually breaks down.
The human brain cannot perform gradient descent.
A biological neuron possesses many dendrites and a single axon, so it can compute only one function – the forward pass.
Gradient descent requires every node to compute two functions: forward and backward.
Moreover, an error signal must somehow travel from the ultimate behavioral outcome back to every neuron.
The brain does contain extensive feedback connections.
The brain certainly does not implement the precise gradient-based credit assignment that artificial networks use.
The architecture of the brain is fundamentally different from artificial networks.
Between every two layers in the brain there are feedback connections.
From later layers in the brain there are connections that reach all the way back.
The brain's feedback connections produce a tangled structure.
We still do not understand the brain's tangled structure in fine detail.
The visual cortex is the part of the cerebral cortex (occipital lobe) that processes visual information.
Hubel and Wiesel pioneered single-neuron recordings in the 1960s–70s.
Hubel and Wiesel won a Nobel Prize.
By attaching tiny electrodes to individual neurons in a live animal, they could read off which visual stimuli made each neuron fire.
Hubel and Wiesel discovered an approximate hierarchical organization in the visual cortex.
V1 processes local features such as oriented lines and edges.
V2 processes more local features and binocular vision.
V3 processes colour, texture, and the first results of segmentation.
V4 processes geometric shapes, silhouettes, and is crucial for attention.
V5 processes the motion of objects segmented in V4.
V6 processes wide-field stimulation, generalizes data from the whole image, and processes changes due to our own movement.
V7 controversially involves recognition of complex objects such as human faces.
Two broad processing streams emerge from the visual cortex: the what pathway and the where pathway.
The what pathway goes from V2 to V4 and is responsible for recognition of shapes and objects.
The where pathway goes from V2 to V5 and V6 and is responsible for motion recognition and control over eyes and hands.
Neurons in V1 have small receptive fields and respond to simple patterns such as a vertical line or a horizontal line.
Neurons in V2 combine inputs from V1 into more complex shapes, for example a corner.
Beyond V2, the clean hierarchy dissolves into a dense mesh of feedback and lateral connections.
There is no simple feed-forward architecture like an artificial CNN beyond V2.
The observation that simple geometric shapes combine hierarchically eventually enabling complex recognition inspired attempts to mimic this in machines.
The first architecture inspired by hierarchical combination of shapes was the neocognitron.
The neocognitron was created by Kunihiko Fukushima in 1979.
The neocognitron was a deep network with convolutional layers.
The neocognitron used hinge-like activations similar to ReLU.
The neocognitron had no learning algorithm; its filters were hand-crafted.
Trainable convolutional networks were created by Yann LeCun's group in the late 1980s.
These trainable convolutional networks already appeared in essentially their modern form.
They used gradient-based learning and convolution operations.
The central assumption behind CNNs is a powerful structural regularisation.
The operation we want to apply to the input is identical everywhere.
If we have a detector that answers a question like "is there a face in this patch?", we apply exactly the same detector to every patch of the image.
The inputs differ from patch to patch, so the answers differ.
The function applied to each patch is shared.
In a CNN, the input is broken into typically overlapping windows.
An image is the easiest data to visualize for this windowing.
The windowing concept works for any data that can be tiled.
A small neural network is applied to every window.
This small network has weights.
This small network is trained by gradient descent.
This small network is extremely small because it sees only a local patch.
A feature map is constructed by arranging the outputs of the small network in the same spatial order as the input windows.
The feature map is a three-dimensional tensor with width, height, and feature depth.
Optionally, the geometry is compressed with a pooling layer.
The pooling layer is usually max pooling.
The output feature tensor can be fed into another convolutional layer.
The output feature tensor is treated as if it were a multi-channel image.
After deep processing, the resulting feature tensor is passed through one or more fully connected layers to produce the final output.
This fully connected part is called a classification head.
The final output can be class probabilities.
Because the small network is applied to every tile, its receptive field is very local.
Stacking convolutions grows the receptive field only additively.
A 3×3 convolution adds 2 pixels of context per layer.
Looking at a 256×256 image with only 3×3 convolutions would require about 130 layers.
The need for many layers is clearly impractical.
This impracticality is the motivation for pooling layers.
A pooling layer takes the feature map and slices it into non-overlapping windows.
Typically, the windows are 2×2.
The pooling layer replaces each window with a single value.
Max pooling takes the maximum value in the window.
Average pooling takes the average value in the window.
Max pooling is far more common in practice than average pooling.
Most features we care about in vision answer "is something present?".
If a head detector outputs 1 for the correct patch and 0 elsewhere, max pooling over a region yields 1 wherever the head appears.
If a head detector outputs 1 for the correct patch and 0 elsewhere, averaging would dilute the signal with all the zeros.
Features that behave as presence detectors naturally compose via max.
Features like average colour would be better served by averaging.
Because convolutional networks are predominantly building shape detectors, max pooling is the default.
With 2×2 pooling, each pooling layer halves the width and halves the height.
With 2×2 pooling, the number of values is reduced by a factor of four.
Alternating convolution and pooling lets the network reach a large receptive field with far fewer layers.
A convolutional layer tiles the input with small windows.
A convolutional layer applies the same transformation to each window independently.
When people say "convolutional layer", they usually mean a single fully connected layer with shared weights inside each window.
The input to a convolutional layer is a three-dimensional tensor of size W×H×D.
D is the feature depth, e.g., D=3 for RGB, D=1 for grayscale.
A tile of size w×h×D is cut out, always taking the full depth.
The tile is flattened into a vector of length D·w·h.
The flattened tile vector is multiplied by a weight matrix W of shape (D·w·h)×d'.
This multiplication produces an output vector of dimension d', the new feature depth for that location.
The crucial property of weight sharing is that exactly the same matrix W is reused for every tile of the input.
In practice, the weights of a convolutional layer are stored as a four-dimensional tensor of shape D×w×h×d' (PyTorch convention).
The input to the convolutional layer is a 3-D tensor matching the first three dimensions.
The output of the convolutional layer is a feature map of depth d'.
The number of trainable parameters in a convolutional layer is D·w·h·d', independent of the full input size.
The classical 2-D convolution formulation is equivalent to the fully connected layer interpretation.
In the 2-D convolution formulation, the linear part is given by y^{(l)}_{i,j} = sum over a,b of W_{a,b} x^{(l)}_{i+a, j+b}.
The notation emphasizes that the same weights W are applied at every position (i,j).
The result y^{(l)}_{i,j} is passed through a nonlinear activation h.
In modern CNNs, the nonlinear activation is almost always ReLU.
The ReLU function is z^{(l)}_{i,j} = max(0, y^{(l)}_{i,j}).
Because each weight is shared across all tiles, it appears many times in the computational graph.
During backpropagation, the gradient for a weight is the sum of gradients across all its occurrences.
The redundancy from weight sharing makes ReLU especially appropriate.
With ReLU, zeroing out some activations still leaves plenty of signal from other tiles for the weight to learn.
A pooling layer with window size (2d+1)×(2d+1) operates on the activated feature map z^{(l)}.
The max pooling operation is x^{(l+1)}_{i,j} = max over a,b of z^{(l)}_{i+a, j+b}.
The windows in a pooling layer are usually non-overlapping.
A 2×2 max-pooling with stride 2 is the most common choice.
Pooling layers contain no trainable parameters.
Pooling layers are deterministic functions.
Convolutional layers are not limited to images.
The idea of cutting input into small tiles and applying a shared weight tensor works for any domain that can be tiled.
1-D convolution on sequences uses an input of size L×D (length × feature depth).
In 1-D convolution, a window of length l slides along the sequence, flattening an l×D tile.
In 1-D convolution, the flattened tile is multiplied by a shared weight tensor of shape l×D×d'.
In 1-D convolution, the output is a vector of size d' per position.
3-D convolution on video uses an input of size t×w×h×D (time × width × height × depth).
In 3-D convolution, the weight tensor is five-dimensional t'×w'×h'×D×d'.
In 3-D convolution, tiles are cut along all spatio-temporal dimensions.
All examples in this lecture series will stay with images.
Convolutions have been especially productive for images.
To see the enormous savings in parameters, we consider a LeNet-style architecture.
The LeNet-style architecture inputs a 32×32 grayscale image.
The input tensor shape is 1×32×32.
Layer 1 is a convolution with kernel size 5×5.
The 5×5 kernel is implied by the output spatial size becoming 28×28 without padding.
Layer 1 convolution has input depth 1 and output depth 6.
The weight tensor for layer 1 is 1×5×5×6.
The number of trainable weights in layer 1 is 150, ignoring biases.
The output tensor of layer 1 is 6×28×28.
A fully connected layer mapping the 32×32 input to a 6×28×28 output would require a weight matrix of size 1024×4704.
That fully connected layer would have about 4.8 million parameters.
The convolutional version uses only 150 parameters, a massive compression.
Weight sharing acts as an excellent structural regularizer.
Layer 2 is a max pooling layer with window 2×2 and non-overlapping.
Layer 2 has no trainable parameters.
The output of layer 2 is 6×14×14.
Each spatial dimension is halved by the max pooling.
Layer 3 is a convolution with kernel 5×5, input depth 6, output depth 16.
A convolutional layer in the network has a weight tensor of shape $6 \times 5 \times 5 \times 16$.
This convolutional layer has 2400 trainable weights, computed as $6 \cdot 25 \cdot 16 = 2400$.
The output tensor has 16 channels and spatial dimensions $10 \times 10$.
No padding is used in this convolutional layer.
The input spatial dimensions are $14 \times 14$.
A $2 \times 2$ max pooling layer is applied next.
The output of the max pooling layer has dimensions $16 \times 5 \times 5$.
The input to the fully connected layers is a flattened vector of $16 \times 5 \times 5 = 400$ values.
The first fully connected layer has 120 neurons and $400 \cdot 120 = 48\,000$ weights.
The second fully connected layer has 84 neurons and $120 \cdot 84 = 10\,080$ weights.
The output layer has 10 neurons and $84 \cdot 10 = 840$ weights.
The output layer uses a softmax activation for classification.
The total number of weights in the network is roughly 60 000.
The vast majority of weights, about 57 000–58 000, reside in the fully connected layers.
The convolutional feature extractor contributes only around 2 500 weights.
Convolutional layers do the heavy lifting of feature extraction while being extremely parameter‑efficient.
Without special treatment, a $K \times K$ convolution reduces spatial dimensions from $W \times H$ to $(W-K+1) \times (H-K+1)$.
Padding adds extra values around the border before convolution to preserve spatial dimensions.
Zero padding surrounds the image with zeros.
Zero padding can create artificial edge responses because the kernel encounters many zeros near the boundary.
Mirror padding reflects edge pixels outward.
Mirror padding avoids introducing spurious zero-valued features.
With padding, a $3 \times 3$ kernel can be centered on any pixel and the output retains the same spatial size.
With stride 1 and padding, the output spatial size is almost the same as the input; without padding, it is slightly reduced.
A stride larger than 1 can reduce spatial dimensions more aggressively without using pooling.
With stride 2, the kernel is placed on every second pixel, yielding an output roughly $W/2 \times H/2$.
Even with a larger stride, every pixel is covered at least once, so no information is lost.
A convolutional layer is defined by its weight tensor shape, padding (type and amount), and stride.
The stride is the step size in each spatial dimension, typically equal for both axes.
Modern convolutional architectures (e.g., Inception, ResNet) use pooling less and instead achieve geometric reduction through strided convolutions.
Pooling can cut off computational paths and distort gradient flow.
Strided convolution is fully differentiable and preserves the shared‑weight linear transform property, unlike pooling.
